items.name: feature-filter-grid
items.title: Feature filter grid
items.description: A grid of many features with chips to filter by area or role, announcing how many are shown and holding its height so nothing jumps.
items.docs: Pass features (an id, an icon, a title, a line, the ids of the groups it belongs to, and optionally an href and a tag) and groups (an id and a label for each chip after All). A chip is only offered when at least one feature belongs to it, and each shows how many features it holds. The chips are a toggle group: arrow keys move between them, Space or Enter chooses, Tab leaves, and choosing the chosen chip again changes nothing. Choosing a chip narrows the grid in place and says, politely, "Showing 7 of 24 features"; the grid keeps the height it had while the new cells arrive and then settles to its own, so the page below does not jump. Under reduced motion it changes at once. A feature can sit in several groups, and one with none shows only under All. With an href the whole cell is a link named by its title; its arrow shows on hover and focus, and always on a touch screen. The cells come in one, two or three columns by the width of the block, not of the screen. Use defaultGroup to start on a chip, or group and onGroupChange to control it ("all" is the id of the first chip), label to name the chips for assistive technology, headingLevel for the heading, and labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: feature-filter-grid-demo
items.title: Feature filter grid demo
items.description: A working preview of Feature filter grid.

items.name: feature-carousel
items.title: Feature carousel
items.description: Feature cards on native scroll snapping with the next card peeking, a counter and arrows, for many features in little room.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and eyebrow, items (an id, an image or an icon, a title, a line and an optional href) and cardWidth (in px, 320 by default). The cards sit on native scroll snapping, so a swipe on a phone and the trackpad on a laptop feel right. The next card always shows by about a quarter of its width: where the width would hide it, or show it nearly whole and cut, the cards are resized a little to make it so. Because the server cannot know the width, the row waits, hidden, until the page has fitted the cards and then fades in, so it never visibly changes size; without scripting it is shown as it is. Pass bleed (a number of px or a CSS length such as "1.5rem" or "var(--page-gutter)", 0 by default) as your page's side padding and the row runs on past the block, so the card that peeks goes off the edge of the screen on a phone instead of stopping at the margin; a variable lets it be 0 where the page has margin to spare. The heading and the Previous and Next buttons share one row where they fit: a short title keeps them beside it on a phone, and a long one sends them to a row of their own below it. The counter ("3 of 8") counts the last card fully in view and follows the real scroll position whether the reader used the buttons, a swipe or the keyboard. It is said politely as it changes, but only once the reader has moved the row, so opening the page announces nothing. The buttons dim at the ends but stay focusable, so keyboard focus is never lost. While the row has focus the arrow keys move one card and Home and End go to the ends; every link inside stays in the tab order. Nothing autoplays, and under reduced motion scrolling is instant. A card with an image shows it in a 16:10 frame; one with an icon and no image gets a tile. A card with an href is a whole-card link named after its title. labels translates the fixed words.

items.title: Feature carousel demo

items.name: feature-with-quote
items.title: Feature with quote
items.description: One feature explained on one side and the customer who proves it on the other: description, points and a quote card with the result.
items.docs: Pass feature (an eyebrow, a title, a description, three points, an href and the link's text) and quote (the words, the name, the role, the company, the address of a picture and the result). The words are a blockquote with the person in its caption: their picture (their initials until it loads, or when there is none), name, job and company. The result is one bold line on a band under the quote, outside it, so it reads as a fact the customer measured and not as something they said; leave it out for a quote without a number. On a phone the feature comes first; reverse swaps the sides from 768px of width. The card sets its padding and type from its own width, so it holds in a narrow column. headingLevel sets the level of the title, and labels translates the word over the result and the button's default text.

items.title: Feature with quote demo
items.description: A working preview of Feature with quote.

items.name: feature-outcomes
items.title: Feature outcomes
items.description: Each feature paired with the result a named customer measured: the feature, what it does and the number it moved.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and eyebrow, items (the feature, an href, a line, the metric as a value and a label, and the customer) and a note. Each row is a ruled line: the feature's name as a link (the whole row is the target), what it does, and on the right a large figure with what was measured and who measured it. The customer is always required, and the note is where you say how the figures were measured and over what period: both are what keep the section honest. Figures use tabular numbers and never wrap, and a word after the number ("11 hrs") is set smaller than the number. A value that starts with a minus or a plus is read out as down or up ("first reply time: down 38%, measured by Northwind"), because a dash is not read as a direction; a hyphen is drawn as a proper minus sign. Under 672px of width each row stacks as feature, description, figure. labels translates up, down and the words read before the customer.

items.title: Feature outcomes demo
items.description: A working preview of Feature outcomes.

items.name: capability-questions
items.title: Capability questions
items.description: The questions sales hears most, answered with a verdict: yes, yes on a plan, not yet, with the how underneath.
items.docs: Pass title, items (a question, a verdict of "yes", "plan", "soon" or "no", the plan's name for a plan verdict, an answer, an href and a group id), groups (an id and a heading each) and contact (a line, a link text and an href). Every answer is on the page: it is a list, not an accordion, so it can be scanned, found with the browser's search and indexed. The verdict is a pill with a word and a shape: a check for Yes, a plus for "On Business", a clock for Not yet and a dash for No, each on its own fill, so none depends on colour. The question is the heading; a screen reader hears it, then the verdict, then the answer. A not-yet or no answer should name what to do instead. The questions sit in two columns from 768px of width and in one under that. With groups, each topic gets a heading one level under the section's and the questions sit one more under it; without, the questions sit directly under the section's heading. labels translates the pills and the docs link.

items.title: Capability questions demo
items.description: A working preview of Capability questions.

items.name: good-fit-section
items.title: Good fit section
items.description: Who it suits and who it does not: two honest columns that save the wrong customers and reassure the right ones.
items.docs: Pass title, fit and notFit (four to six short lines each), alternative (the line and its href) and cta (a label and an href). Two columns sit on one bordered surface under "A good fit if" with checks and "Probably not if" with dashes; the second is tinted so it reads as the quieter one. The action sits under the first list and, under the second, a line points to what to use instead; the whole line is the link when you give an href. Both lists are real lists under real headings, and the check and dash icons repeat what the headings already say, so they are hidden from assistive technology. Under 768px of width the columns stack with the good fit first. align centres the heading; labels translates the two column heads.

items.name: deployment-options
items.title: Deployment options
items.description: Cloud, self-hosted or hybrid side by side: who runs it, where data lives, what you manage and who it is for.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description, and two to four options: an id, a name, a bestFor line that finishes "Best for ...", facts as label and value pairs, one cta and recommended. Use the same fact labels, in the same order, in every option. On a wide block every card is a subgrid over the same rows, so the Nth fact of every card sits on one line and each row is as tall as its tallest answer; under that the cards stack, each a column of facts, with the label beside its answer from 576px of width and above it on a phone. An option that lacks a fact the others have shows a dash, so the rows still line up. Recommended is written on the card, which also gets a heavier border and a solid button. No price appears: this is about fit, not billing. Two options sit side by side from 672px of width, three from 896px, and four go two by two and then four across from 1152px. align centres the heading; labels translates the fixed words.

items.name: platform-availability
items.title: Platform availability
items.description: Where it runs: web, iOS, Android, desktop and API as tiles with status, version and a link to get it.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description, platforms and a footnote. Each platform has an id, a label, an icon, a status ("available", "beta" or "soon"), an optional version and releasedAt (an ISO date, written in the locale and timeZone you pass), an href with a linkLabel ("Open the app", "App Store", "Download") and a note. The status is a pill with its word and a shape, never colour alone. A tile with a link is a whole-tile link named after its platform. A coming-soon tile has no download: pass an href and it becomes a plain link to a waiting list ("Tell me when it is ready" unless you give a linkLabel). The tiles are a list, so a screen reader hears how many there are. Edit the data and the page stays honest; visitors stop asking whether there is an Android app. labels translates the status words and the fixed text.

items.name: api-endpoints
items.title: API endpoints
items.description: Every endpoint of an API at a glance, grouped by resource: the method as a word, the path with parameters dimmed, a one-line job and a link to the reference.
items.docs: Pass groups (a label and its endpoints, each with a method, a path, a one-line description and an href), plus baseUrl for the copy field over the list and docsHref for the link beside the heading. The method is always a word in a fixed-width label: GET is quiet and outlined, POST is solid, PATCH and PUT are a strong outline and DELETE a strong dashed one, so nothing depends on colour. Parameters written as {id} or :id are dimmed in the path. Chips filter by method, show how many endpoints each holds, and a polite status says how many are on screen; a method nothing uses is never offered. Use defaultMethod to start on a chip, or method and onMethodChange to control it. On a wide block a row is four columns; on a narrow one it stacks as method and path, then the description and the link. A base URL too long for its line wraps under its button instead of hiding behind a scrollbar. Words are translated through labels.

items.title: API endpoints demo
items.description: A working preview of API endpoints.

items.name: sdk-grid
items.title: SDK grid
items.description: Official libraries as cards: language, version, a written status, a copyable install command and links to docs and source, plus a card for community libraries.
items.docs: Pass sdks (an id, a label, the install command, the version, a status of stable, beta or community, and the docs and source links) and, optionally, communityHref for a last dashed card that says plainly those libraries are not official. The status is always a word with its own shape: a check for Stable, a flask for Beta, a group for Community. The install command is real text in a copy field, and each copy button is named after its language, so a page of eight does not give a screen reader eight identical buttons. A command that does not fit beside its button wraps, with the button under it, instead of hiding behind a scrollbar. Give an sdk a mark (a logo or glyph at 22px) or let the card show the first letters of its name. The block has no state of its own and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

items.title: SDK grid demo
items.description: A working preview of SDK grid.

items.name: quickstart-steps
items.title: Quickstart steps
items.description: Up and running in three commands: numbered steps, each with a copyable command and what you should see, and a package manager switch.
items.docs: Pass steps (a title, the command, optionally what the terminal should print and a one-line note) and, optionally, next for the last node that links on. Add variants, one list of commands per package manager in step order, to get a switch in the heading, over the steps; a step a list leaves out keeps its own command, and the switch says politely which commands it is showing. Where the output depends on the package manager, give expected as an object keyed like variants: the reader sees the output of the manager they chose. Every copy button is named with its step number and title, the expected output is plain text that can be selected, and nothing is tracked or stored: use manager and onManagerChange if you want the choice remembered. A command that does not fit beside its button wraps, with the button under it. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: trust-documents
items.title: Trust documents
items.description: The documents a security review asks for, each with its date and size, as a download or a request that opens a short form and calls your handler.
items.docs: Pass documents (an id, a title, a line about it, the format, the size, the date it applies to, access as public or request, and the href of a public file) and onRequest, called with the document id and the checked details (email and company) when someone asks for one. Resolve it to confirm; reject it to show an error that keeps everything typed. A public document is a real download link whose name carries the title, the type and the size; one on request is marked in words and opens a dialog that checks a work email and a company, confirms with a focused status message, and afterwards reads Requested. A request in flight cannot be closed away, so its failure is never lost, and on a short screen the dialog keeps a margin and scrolls inside itself, so its title and the retry button can always be reached. On a wide block the date and the size get a column of their own. Nothing is sent or stored by the block. Use contact for the line under the list and the fallback in the error, locale and timeZone for the dates, and labels to translate every word, error messages included.

items.title: Trust documents demo
items.description: A working preview of Trust documents.

items.name: service-levels
items.title: Service levels
items.description: Commitments in numbers: response times by priority, each defined in a sentence, and uptime targets with the downtime they allow and the credit owed.
items.docs: Pass support (a priority code, an optional name, a one-sentence definition, the first response, the update interval and the channels) and availability (the uptime target, what it allows per month, the service credit and optionally the plan it belongs to). Add hours for the line under the tables that says when support applies, and slaHref for a link to the full agreement. The two tables sit side by side from 76rem, the inside of an 80rem page container, and stack on anything narrower so neither column is cramped; both switch together between real tables and lists of cards with the same labels, so on a phone nothing hides in a horizontal scroll. Figures are tabular, and both tables have captions. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: which-one-guide
items.title: Which one guide
items.description: If you are this, pick that: scenario rows that point each kind of buyer to the right plan, model or product.
items.docs: Pass rows (a scenario in the reader's own voice and the recommendation: a name, a one-line reason and a link) and, optionally, a fallback for the reader nobody wrote a sentence for. A row reads scenario, arrow, then the option as a chip with its reason; on a medium block it is two columns, the scenario beside the answer, with the arrow leading into the chip; on a narrow block the arrow turns downward and the answer sits under the scenario. The chip names the option in words and screen readers hear Recommended before it. It is a static decision aid with no quiz and no state, so it renders on the server and works with JavaScript off. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: industry-index
items.title: Industry index
items.description: Twelve to thirty industries as a compact index grouped by sector, each a link with a quiet customer count, and an optional live search.
items.docs: Pass sectors (a label and its industries, each with a name, an href, optionally a customer count and a featured flag). A featured industry leads its sector and is marked Popular in words; counts are tabular, quiet and read out as customers. Lists flow into one, two or three columns by the width of the block, and no industry is split across two. Set filterable to add a search field that narrows the index as you type and says how many are left; when nothing matches it says so and offers the contact link. Use locale for the numbers and labels to translate every word.

items.name: import-sources
items.title: Import sources
items.description: Where your data can come from: the tools you can import from, what comes across and how long it takes.
items.docs: Pass sources (an id, the tool's name, an optional mark, what comes across as short names, a time estimate in plain words and the link to its import guide), plus csv for a closing dashed tile and help for the line under the grid. Each tile is one link: the name is a link stretched over the tile, named by the tool and import guide. The chips and the estimate say only what you pass in. A tool without a mark shows its first letter. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: two-sided-features
items.title: Two sided features
items.description: A platform explained to both sides: what buyers get and what sellers get, mirrored around a centre line, each side with benefits and an action of its own.
items.docs: Pass sides, a pair of audiences: each has a label ("For hosts"), a heading, benefits (an icon, a title and a description) and a cta. The benefits sit on the same rows across the centre rule, so each pair reads straight across, and both sides get the same button, so neither reads as an afterthought. On a narrow block the sides stack with a labelled divider between them (the word is labels.and). The heading is centred by default; align="start" sets it from the left. The heading of each side is always set smaller than the title, at level 3 as at level 2, so the title stays the focal point. The block has no state and renders on the server.

items.name: extension-points
items.title: Extension points
items.description: How far you can bend the product, from no-code to code: custom fields, rules, webhooks, plugins and the API, each with its level, examples and a guide.
items.docs: Pass levels (an id, a label and, if you like, a description) from the least technical to the most, and points (a name, the id of its level, a description, example chips and a guide link). The levels set the order of the ladder, so it can never be shown upside down, and the level is always written out beside the name. A step marker on the left grows by one bar on every row; it is decoration and hidden from assistive technology, because the list is an ordered list. When any level has a description a key above the ladder says what each level takes; the levels sit in equal columns by their number, or stack, and never as two and one. Add a footnote for the promise that answers the fear of lock-in. The block has no state and renders on the server.

items.name: stack-layers
items.title: Stack layers
items.description: Your architecture as horizontal layers, edge to storage: each with its technologies, a one-line promise and a metric, along a rail that marks a request's path.
items.docs: Pass layers in the order a request meets them: an id, a name, the technologies as chips, a one-line promise and, if you have one, a metric (a value and what it measures). The block is an ordered list read from top to bottom; the metric is plain text, and the rail on the left is decoration that marks the path of a request. On a wide block the layers are bands separated by hairlines; on a narrow one each becomes a card, joined to the next by a short line. A layer without a metric simply has none. Add a footnote for where the figures come from. Nothing animates, the block has no state and it renders on the server.

items.name: region-list
items.title: Region list
items.description: Where your data can live: regions by continent with city, status, latency and compliance tags in a real, filterable table, not a map.
items.docs: Pass regions (a code, a city, a country, a continent, a status of available, beta or planned, latencyMs and tags) and latencyFrom, the place the latency is measured from. Chips filter by tag, show how many regions each holds and say politely how many are on screen; a tag no region carries is never offered. Use defaultTag to start on a chip, or tag and onTagChange to control it. A planned region has no latency and the row says so. On a wide block the list is a real table with headers and a caption, grouped by continent, whose columns hold their places while a chip filters; on a narrow one every region is a card with the latency written out ("about 12 ms from Amsterdam"). Add selectHref, with {code} for the region's code, to give each live region a link. Words are translated through labels and numbers follow locale.

items.name: model-lineup
items.title: Model lineup
items.description: A model family compared on what matters: best for, context window, speed and price per million tokens, with one model marked Recommended in words.
items.docs: Pass models (an id, a name, a tier, bestFor, context in tokens, speed from 1 to 3, priceIn and priceOut per million tokens, an href and, for the one you would pick first, recommended), plus currency and locale for the prices. Context is written compactly ("200K") and every figure is tabular. Speed is a three-segment meter with a word beside it: Fast, Faster or Fastest, never the meter alone. On a wide block the models are rows of a real table with a caption, where the row header is the model's name, its tier and the Recommended mark, and what it is best for has a column of its own; the column of links is left out when no model has an href. On a narrow block each is a card with the same labels. Add a note under it for billing details. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

items.description: A working preview of Model lineup.

items.name: sync-mapping
items.title: Sync mapping
items.description: What syncs between two tools: object pairs, direction, how often and what stays manual, in a clear table with the limits listed underneath.
items.docs: Pass left and right (a name and an optional mark for each tool), rows (your object, theirs, a direction of to-right, to-left or both, a frequency and an optional note) and limits, a plain list of what does not sync. The direction is drawn as an arrow and written out, and a screen reader hears it in full ("Contacts to Customers, two way"). The table scrolls sideways in a region of its own on a narrow block, which can be focused and scrolled with the keyboard, and says so underneath. The first column, your object, stays pinned while it scrolls, so a row never loses its name. The region is a tab stop at every width, also where the table fits: a scroller that cannot be reached by keyboard is worse, and knowing that it overflows takes a script. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: automation-recipes
items.title: Automation recipes
items.description: Ready-made automations as trigger and action rows: when this happens, do that, with the apps named and a button to use the recipe, under tabs by team.
items.docs: Pass recipes (an id, an outcome, a trigger with app and event, and one to three actions with app and action) and onUse, which is called with the recipe's id and the recipe when its button is pressed; the block starts nothing itself. Add groups (an id and a label each, with a group on every recipe) to put the recipes under tabs by team. Each row is a list item with the outcome as its heading, and app names are plain text with no logos. The chips wrap on a narrow block and the arrow turns to point down. Use defaultGroup, or group and onGroupChange, to choose the tab. Words are translated through labels.

items.name: materials-section
items.title: Materials section
items.description: What it is made of and where it comes from: materials with share, origin and certification beside a short story, for products that must prove it.
items.docs: Pass a title, a story and materials (a name, a share in percent, an origin, an optional certification and a swatch, a CSS colour for the material's own tone), plus care, a short list for washing or maintenance. The share is written as text first and the thin bar under it is decoration, hidden from assistive technology. The shares should add up to 100: while you develop, the block warns in the console when they do not. Origins are plain places and a certification is a word in a badge. The halves sit side by side by the width of the block. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels, and the shares follow locale.

items.name: certifications-explained
items.title: Certifications explained
items.description: Labels in plain words: what each certification means, who issues it, its number and where to verify it, as cards with a description list.
items.docs: Pass certifications (an id, a name, an issuer, a meaning in one plain sentence, and optionally a number, since, a verifyHref and a mark) and a footnote. Each card has the name as its heading with the issuer under it, and a description list so the facts read as pairs. The number is set in monospace, a since that is a day is written in the locale and time zone you pass, and a fact you leave out is simply not shown. The Verify link opens in a new tab and says so to screen readers. No seal image is required: without a mark, a typographic one is drawn from the name. The columns follow the number of labels: one is a single card, two or four sit in pairs, and any other number fills three columns on a wide block, so no column is left empty. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

items.title: Certifications explained demo
items.description: A working preview of Certifications explained.

items.name: spend-breakdown
items.title: Spend breakdown
items.description: Where every 100 goes: a ten-by-ten unit chart in tones and patterns, beside a legend that says what each share pays for.
items.docs: Pass title, description, parts (up to six, largest first, each with an id, a label, a share and a sentence on what it pays for) and optionally total (the whole as an amount, with a currency and a few words such as raised in 2025) and source (who says so, a link and a year). The shares are read as percentages of a hundred, and if they do not add up to 100 they are scaled, so the grid is always full. The hundred squares are allotted by the largest remainder method: 33.4, 33.3 and 33.3 become 34, 33 and 33 squares, the grid is exactly full, and the legend keeps the exact figures. Every part has a tone and a pattern of its own (solid, hatch, dots, cross hatch, a mid tone with sparse lines, vertical lines), so the chart still reads in greyscale and in print and no part looks like an empty square. The squares are hidden from assistive technology; the table beside them, with each percentage, name and sentence, is the content. Hovering a row of the legend keeps its squares lit and dims the rest, with no script. The percentage of a row is its row header, so a screen reader names a sentence by its share and not by the whole sentence. The legend sits beside the squares from 768px of width and under them on a narrower section, and on a small phone it gives up some padding so the sentences keep their room. Amounts are written short (€3.44M, €462K) with their digits pinned, so the server and the browser print the same text; where a locale's own data differs between the two runtimes (en-GB writes €4.2M in one and €4.2m in another) the figures are marked so the server's text stays and the page is not rebuilt. labels translates the fixed words, and the section renders on the server.

items.name: commitments-progress
items.title: Commitments progress
items.description: Public goals with their progress: target, current value, deadline and last-updated date, in rows a reader can check.
items.docs: Pass title, description, groups (a heading and its commitments; each commitment has an id, a title, the current and target values with an optional unit, a deadline written as 2028, 2028-06 or 2028-12-31, a status of done, on-track, at-risk or missed, and an optional note), updatedAt (required) and reportHref. Each row shows its progress as a labelled progressbar whose value text is the same figures written out (62% of 100%, or 4 of 6 warehouses when the unit is a word), the deadline in a time element and the status as a chip with a word and an icon, so nothing depends on colour: weight does the telling, with at risk the solid chip and missed the destructive one (its text is darkened in the light theme to keep AA contrast). A tally under the heading counts the commitments in each state. The date of the last update is always shown, and once it is older than staleAfterDays (180 by default), measured against the now you pass or the current time, the section says so in words. The current time is the moment the section renders, so a page that is generated once shows the note only as of its build: revalidate it on a schedule, or pass a now that you keep fresh. Rows stack on a phone and sit in three columns from 768px of width. State each goal as a number that grows towards its target, such as a cut achieved. labels translates the fixed words, and locale and timeZone format the numbers and dates.

The tiers are an ordered list joined by a rail: columns from 768px of width for up to three tiers and from 896px for four, and one under the other with the rail on the left below that. Without more it is the ladder a visitor sees and nothing is marked. Give it the member's tier as current and how far they are as progress (a value and nextAt, with a currency such as EUR or a unit such as months) and their own tier carries aria-current and the words Your tier, the tiers below it say Reached, the rail is filled up to a marker between the member's tier and the next, and a progress bar says the same in numbers and in words, such as 180 euros to go until Gold. The rail is decoration; everything it shows is also said in text. labels translates the fixed words and locale formats the numbers.

items.name: rollout-plan
items.title: Rollout plan
items.description: What happens after you sign: a timeline from day one to day ninety, with who does what at each point.
items.docs: Pass title, description, milestones (four to six, each with a time label such as Day 1 or Week 2, a title, a sentence and an owner of us, you or both) and optionally a note for the fine print about what the dates assume. The first milestone is marked Start and the last Outcome, in words under its time label; flag another milestone with outcome to move the payoff. The time labels and owners are text, and the spine is a hairline between a filled start, open markers and a filled outcome, never an image, so order and ownership read without colour. On a wide section the heading sits beside the plan and each row has three columns (time, spine, milestone); on a phone the time label stacks above the title. It is an ordered list, so a screen reader announces each step's position. labels translates the fixed words, so Us and You can read Halcyon and Your team.

items.name: app-screens-row
items.title: App screens row
items.description: A row of CSS-drawn phone frames with a caption under each, the middle one larger, scrolling sideways with snap on a phone.
items.docs: Pass title, description and screens (four to six, each with a src, alt text, a caption, the image's width and height, and optionally a srcSet, sizes, a blurDataUrl and priority). Every screen is a figure with a caption, in a phone drawn in CSS that follows both themes and costs no bytes; the screenshots are shown on a 9:19.5 screen, so crop them to that. On a section 896px wide or more the row is a grid in which the featured screen (the middle one, or featuredIndex) is larger and the others stand on the same line, a little lower, with their captions level; below that it is a sideways scroller that snaps to a screen and lets the next one peek in. The scroller is a region named App screens that the keyboard can reach and scroll with the arrow keys, Home and End, and it is a stop in the tab order only while there is something to scroll. With a mouse it shows a thin scrollbar to drag, and on touch the scrollbar is hidden. Give each row its own labels.region when a page has more than one. Pass bleed (your page's side padding) and the scroller runs to the edge of the screen on a phone. Pictures keep their proportions before they load, show a blurred seed from blurDataUrl until they arrive and are lazy unless priority is set; renderImage plugs in next/image. Only the scroll region is a client component.

items.name: keyboard-features
items.title: Keyboard features
items.description: A keyboard-first product's shortcuts as cards: the keys, what they do, and a card that lights up when you press them.
items.docs: Pass title, description, shortcuts (six to nine, each with an id, keys, a verb-first title and a line of detail) and optionally cta, platform and preventDefault. Keys are written as text: Mod+K is a chord (Mod is Cmd on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere), G then P is a sequence, and ? or Esc are single keys; the modifiers are Mod, Ctrl, Alt, Shift and Meta. Press a real shortcut while no field has focus and its card lights for a second, its keys turn solid and its title is announced politely; in a sequence the first key lights and the second has a moment to follow. Under reduced motion the card gets a bold outline instead and nothing lifts, fades or flips. platform is auto by default, which reads the keyboard after hydration, so until then Mod is written Cmd/Ctrl and no reader is shown a key they do not have; mac and other fix it. Mac symbols come with their spoken names, so every key is also text. Keys are never taken from the browser unless preventDefault is set. The helpers that parse and match shortcuts live in keys.ts, which needs no client code. labels translates the fixed words.

items.name: prompt-examples
items.title: Prompt examples
items.description: What an AI feature can do, shown as written prompts and answers, with a tab per task and a Try this prompt action.
items.docs: Pass title, description and examples (three to five, each with an id, a tab label and optional icon, the prompt, the answer and an optional note), and onTry to hand a prompt to your product; without onTry the action is not shown. The answer is any content you write, dressed as prose, so plain paragraphs, lists and strong text are enough and a Table sits in it as it is. Static and honest: nothing is generated, so it needs no key and has no rate limit, and a note such as Example output, edited for length is only shown when you pass one. The tabs are real tabs with arrow keys and roving focus, controlled with value and onValueChange or left to open on defaultValue. All the panels share one cell of a grid and only the open one is visible, so the section is as tall as its tallest answer and nothing below it jumps; the closed answers stay in the page but are hidden from the screen and the keyboard. Tab icons show from 512px of width, and below 340px the tabs give up some padding and a point of type so all four fit on a small phone. Try this prompt always sits at the end of its line, with or without a note, and a panel's focus outline wraps its own answer. labels translates the fixed words.

items.name: tour-chapters
items.title: Tour chapters
items.description: A product video with its chapters beside it: pick a topic and the video jumps there and plays, with each start time written out.
items.docs: Pass title, src (one address, or several files of different formats), poster, captions (a WebVTT address), transcriptHref and chapters, each with a start in seconds, a title and an optional description (two lines of it are shown, the rest is cut with an ellipsis). The video is a native player with controls and a captions track, and only its first frames and its length are fetched until someone plays it. Beside it, every chapter is a button named like "Chapter 3 of 6, 1:42, Invite your team": a click, a tap, Enter or Space jumps to that time and plays. The chapter the video is in is marked (its time turns solid, its row is filled and a hairline fills along it, and it carries aria-current), and the list keeps it in view without moving the page. The arrow keys, Home and End move between chapters. On a wide screen the list is as tall as the player and scrolls, and its scroll box is not a tab stop of its own (the chapters are the stops); on a phone it follows the player at full length, and picking a chapter far down it scrolls the player back into view, so the jump is seen. onChapterSelect reports the chapter a visitor picks, and labels carries the fixed words for another language.

items.name: locale-demo
items.title: Locale demo
items.description: Show localisation instead of claiming it: pick a language and the same price, date, number and plural change shape live.
items.docs: Pass title, a sample (amount and currency, an ISO date, a count and, if you like, a number and a number of days) and optionally description, locales (a code and a label each), defaultLocale and timeZone. English, Dutch, German, Japanese and Arabic are built in, with the card's own words; for another language pass messages with its locale. Every value is made by Intl (NumberFormat, DateTimeFormat in the time zone you give, RelativeTimeFormat and PluralRules) and shown with the raw value it came from, as a caption under it. The card turns around for languages written from right to left, the switch wraps into evenly sized rows on a phone, and it is announced as "Showing Deutsch". locale and onLocaleChange control it from outside.

items.name: theme-preview
items.title: Theme preview
items.description: A product screen inside a frame with its own theme, and a switch between light, dark and high contrast, so theming is something visitors can see.
items.docs: Pass title and, optionally, description, themes, defaultTheme and children. The frame carries data-theme, redefines the semantic tokens on itself (background, foreground, card, border, ring and the rest) and sets color-scheme, so everything in it follows while the page keeps its own theme. Only the semantic tokens (and [data-theme] selectors) follow the frame: a dark: variant in your own markup still follows the page's dark mode, so scope it to the frame with @custom-variant dark (&:is(.dark *):not(.light *)); the frame carries a light or dark class for that. Light, dark and high contrast have colours built in; give a theme tokens (a map of custom properties) to show your own palette, and children to draw your own screen instead of the sample. The sample is made of RHS UI's own components, so hover, focus and press work in every theme. The switch is announced as "Showing the Dark theme"; theme and onThemeChange control it from outside.

items.description: One figure as the picture: a huge number at the largest size its container allows, what it measures, a dated source and the action that follows.
items.docs: value is the figure, unit what it counts ("million litres", "years", "%"), label what it measures, and format takes options for Intl.NumberFormat, such as { maximumFractionDigits: 1 } or { style: "percent" }. The figure is set at the largest size its container allows, from a phone to a wide page: a short unit stays beside it, a longer one drops under it on a narrow screen. The heading holds the label and the final value as text from the first render. animate counts up from zero once, the first time the figure is on screen, using AnimatedNumber; duration is in seconds; under reduced motion, or without IntersectionObserver, the final value is simply there. source is words or { label, href }, asOf the day the figure was true (shown in a time element) and actions the buttons, the first of them solid. Pass locale and timeZone, and labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: gallery-hero
items.title: Gallery hero
items.description: A full-bleed photograph opening a series: the picture, caption and credit, a counter with Previous and Next, and thumbnails that switch it.
items.docs: photos is an array of { src, alt, title, place?, year?, credit? } and initial the index shown first; give each photo srcSet and sizes for responsive files and thumb for a small file in the strip, so a series of large pictures does not load them all as thumbnails. The caption bar writes the title and place on the left, the year and credit on the right, and a "03 / 08" counter beside Previous and Next. A strip of thumbnails switches the picture, and so do the arrow keys, Home and End while focus is inside the gallery, and a swipe on a touch screen. A new picture fades in over the old one, the pictures either side are fetched ahead, the caption is announced through a polite live region, and no timer ever advances it. title stays small in a corner so the photograph carries the page; cta adds a link in the other corner. onIndexChange(index) tells your page which picture is showing; it is a function, so use the hero inside a Client Component then. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

items.name: community-hero
items.title: Community hero
items.description: A community opening built from its members: a mosaic of faces, the member count, the channels busy right now and one join button.
items.docs: Pass twelve to eighteen members (name and an optional square image): the first half sit on the left of the text and the rest on the right, a phone shows eight, and a member without a picture is drawn as initials. Pictures load lazily, so the faces a phone hides are never fetched. total is the figure on the line under the button, channels are the ones busy now with how many are in each, and joinHref is where the button goes. The mosaic is decoration: a screen reader gets one sentence naming the first few members, and the labels prop translates it with the other fixed words. The faces flank the text when the container is at least 68rem wide and become a row above and below it otherwise, so the hero follows the width of its parent, not the window.

items.title: Creator hero
items.description: A link-in-bio opening for a creator: avatar, handle, a line of bio, three audience numbers and a column of link buttons, designed at 320px.
items.docs: Give name, handle, bio and an optional square avatar (without one the initials are drawn). stats are numbers, not strings: 48200 is shown as 48.2K in the locale you pass and read in full to a screen reader. links is the stack of buttons: a label, an href, an icon from @rhs-ui/icons, an optional badge ("new", "beta" or "soon") and featured for the one link to set in solid colour. A link to an absolute http(s) address opens in a new tab with rel="noopener noreferrer" and says so to screen readers; pass external to override. socials are profiles named in text, not logos. items.name: breathing-hero
items.title: Breathing hero
items.description: A wellness opening with a ring that breathes in, holds and out on a 4-4-6 rhythm, the words to match, a pause control and a start button.
items.docs: pattern is seconds in, hold and out (4, 4 and 6 by default; a hold of 0 skips it). The ring is moved by CSS animations whose length comes from the pattern, so no script runs per frame; one timer wakes at each change of phase to update the words and the status announcement, which is polite and stops while paused. A Pause and Resume button is always there: leave paused out to let it work, or pass paused and onPausedChange to control it. onStart is called when the main button is pressed, or pass ctaHref to make it a link. Under reduced motion the ring stays still and the words and a thin progress line in three named parts (In 4s, Hold 4s, Out 6s) carry the timing. onStart is a function, so use the hero inside a Client Component. A pattern you change while it runs takes effect from the current phase; give the hero a new key to start again from the first breath. labels translates the fixed words, the three timing captions included ({count} stands for the seconds). Any other prop, such as an id for a nav anchor, aria or data attributes or a ref, goes to the section.

items.name: navbar-centered-logo
items.title: Centered logo navbar
items.description: A navbar with the mark on the true middle, links on the left and actions on the right, folding into a menu button on a phone.
items.docs: The props match Navbar (brand, items, actions, currentHref, linkAs, sticky), so one can replace the other: items are links, or groups that open as panels in the shared navigation menu. The three zones are one grid, so the brand stays on the true middle. The links only sit beside it where they fit: a side of the bar has room for about three short links at 768px, five at 1024px and six at 1280px, and no more than that at any width. The bar folds them into the sheet below the width that suits their number (md up to three links, lg for four, xl beyond that, so keep the list to six); pass foldBelow (md, lg or xl) to choose it yourself, for a wide mark or long labels. The current page gets aria-current and a thin underline that grows from the centre on hover and focus. Where the links fold they move into a sheet opened from the menu button on the left (menuLabel names it), and below md the actions fold into one icon button on the right that opens them in a popover; actionsLabel names the button and the popover, and actionsIcon changes its icon. Pass linkAs={Link} for your router's links.

items.name: navbar-with-search
items.title: Navbar with search
items.description: A navbar built around a search field that opens your command palette, with an icon button in its place on a phone.
items.docs: The field is a real button: it calls onSearchOpen, so open your own command palette or search overlay there and the bar keeps no search logic. It shows the shortcut for the platform (the Command symbol on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere) with the letter from shortcutKey, and the shortcut works anywhere on the page, also below lg where the field gives way to an icon button named by searchLabel. Under md the links move into a sheet with the actions at its foot. onSearchOpen is a function, so use the bar from a Client Component, next to the palette it opens. Pass linkAs={Link} for your router's links and currentHref to mark the current page, and navLabel and menuLabel to name the navigation landmark and the phone menu (its button and its sheet).

items.name: navbar-transparent
items.title: Transparent navbar
items.description: A navbar that sits over the hero with no background and turns solid with a hairline as soon as the page scrolls.
items.docs: The bar is fixed to the top of the window and see-through at rest, so put it over a hero that is already dark (tone="light", the default) or light (tone="dark"). Once the page has scrolled past threshold (24px) it takes the page colour and a hairline. One passive scroll listener sets data-scrolled on the header for your own styling, and the state starts from the real scroll position. At rest with a light tone the text is white and the bar speaks the dark theme's tokens, so buttons you pass as actions are legible on a photograph; a theme with no dark tokens should give those buttons colours of their own. Once solid the bar hands everything back to the page. The phone menu opens on a solid sheet; navLabel names the navigation landmark, and menuLabel the menu button and the title of the sheet. In a layout that scrolls inside a container, the bar follows that container instead of the window: pass className="sticky -mb-16" so the hero still slides under it. Pass scrolled to fix the state for a preview or a test.

items.name: navbar-onepage
items.title: One-page navbar
items.description: A navbar for single-page sites: section links that scroll to their section, the current one marked, and one call to action.
items.docs: Give sections as an id and a label each, in the order they appear; every link is a real fragment link, so it works before script loads. Give each section scroll-mt-20 (as tall as offset, 80px by default) so a visitor who arrives with the hash in the address also clears the bar. The section in view is marked with aria-current="location" as you scroll; pass currentId to mark one yourself. A click scrolls smoothly (instantly under reduced motion), moves focus to the section's heading and calls onNavigate. On a phone the links are in a sheet that closes itself before the scroll. The mark links to brandHref ("#top" scrolls to the top and drops the hash of the section you were in); a call to action with href="#contact" scrolls like the rest. onNavigate is a function, so use the bar from a Client Component.

items.title: Footer with link rows
items.description: A footer that sets link groups as labelled rows instead of columns, for sites with a few short groups and room to breathe.
items.docs: Each group is a label and its links; the label sits on the left and the links run inline to its right, wrapping naturally, and on a phone the label sits above them. Every group is a list named by its own heading, all inside one Footer navigation. A link with external: true opens in a new tab and says so. social profiles show as round icon links when you give an icon from @rhs-ui/icons and as text links when you do not. Pass linkAs={Link} for your router's links, and navLabel and labels to translate the fixed words. items.description: A footer for large sites: up to six link columns that fold into tap-to-open groups on a phone, with a bar for social and legal.
items.docs: Give up to six columns, each with a title and groups of links; a group may have a heading of its own. From md up everything is visible. Below md each column is a button with aria-expanded and a plus or a minus, and defaultOpen lists the titles that start open. The desktop heading and the phone button are separate elements, and the links are in the page either way, closed or not. Columns animate their height and snap open under reduced motion. aside is a slot beside the brand (a newsletter, a status link), social takes icon or text profiles, and legal with legalLinks fills the bottom bar. items.name: mobile-nav-drilldown
items.title: Drill-down mobile menu
items.description: A phone menu where each group slides its links in as a new panel with a Back row, the way native apps navigate.
items.docs: Pass brand, the groups and, if you like, actions (sign in, start free) and current, the href of the page you are on. A group with links opens as a panel of its own; a group without links is a plain link, and one with links and an href offers an All row first that leads to the group's own page. Every link closes the sheet. Escape goes up a level before it closes the sheet, Up, Down, Home and End move between the rows, and the panels you cannot see are inert, so their links are never tabbable. DrilldownMenu is the same menu without the sheet, for a container of your own, and defaultGroup opens one panel first. The menu button is shown at every width: pass className="md:hidden" to hide it from md up, or trigger to use a button of your own. open, defaultOpen and onOpenChange control the sheet, labels translates the fixed words, and linkAs renders your router's Link. onOpenChange is a function, so use the menu from a Client Component if you control it.

items.name: utility-bar
items.title: Utility bar
items.description: A slim bar above the header with the practical things: phone, email, an open-now line in words, and language and login links.
items.docs: Give it phone, email, status and links. The phone and the email are tel: and mailto: links whose text is the number and the address themselves, so they can be read, copied and printed; phoneHref sets another tel: address for a number with an extension. status is the shape OpeningHours takes, { open, text }, worked out on your side from your clock in the business's time zone: the bar shows your words with a filled dot when open and a hollow one when closed, so it never leans on colour. Below sm only the phone and the status show; the email appears from sm and the links, which belong in the main menu on a phone, from md. Between md and lg the email makes way for the links, so the bar stays one row on a tablet, and it returns from lg. With no phone and no status the bar is not drawn where it would be empty: below md when it holds only links, below sm when it holds only an email. A link in another language takes lang, so a screen reader pronounces it right. linkAs renders your router's Link and labels translates the fixed words.

items.name: breadcrumb-bar
items.title: Breadcrumb bar
items.description: A slim bar under the header with the trail on the left and page actions on the right, folding to a single Back link on a phone.
items.docs: Pass the trail from the top, the last crumb being the current page, which carries aria-current and is not a link. From md up the bar shows the ordered list; once it is longer than maxItems (4) the first crumb and the last ones stay and the levels between fold into a menu with a link each. Below md it is one Back link to the nearest parent that has an href. The trail has priority on the row: its crumbs never wrap, every crumb but the current page keeps its width (a very long label is cut at 10rem with an ellipsis) and only the current page gives way when the row runs short. actions is a slot for small buttons or links such as Share, Print or Edit; updated takes the words you format, in the language and time zone of the page, and the same moment as a machine-readable dateTime; it shows from lg up, where there is room for it beside the trail and the actions. labels translates the fixed words and linkAs renders your router's Link.

items.title: App store footer
items.description: A footer with link columns, the two store buttons drawn in the house style and a QR code slot for visitors at a desk.

Under sm the buttons stack at the full width and a 48px height. qr is any node, an img or an svg dark on a clear ground; it shows from lg on a white tile, because a scanner needs a light margin in both themes, and a screen reader skips it, as it has the links. items.title: Local business footer
items.description: A footer for a shop, practice or tradesperson: address, phone, today's opening hours, a route button and the registration line.
items.docs: address is an array of lines, set in a real address element with the phone and the email, whose links carry the number and the address as their own text; phoneHref sets another tel: address for a number with an extension. hours takes the shape OpeningHours takes: the days, today's index and the open-now line, which you work out in the business's time zone. The footer draws the week itself, so its heading, the word read out after today and the word for a closed day are all in labels. routeHref opens in a new tab and says so; routeNote adds a line beside the button and map takes a static map image or a drawing, which is hidden from assistive technology, so put nothing in it a visitor needs. registration lists the numbers a Dutch or German site shows, such as KvK, BTW, HRB or USt-IdNr., as a definition list in the legal row. labels translates the headings, the words of the hours and the route button, and linkAs renders your router's Link.

items.title: Region footer
items.description: A footer with a built-in region picker: country, language and currency chosen from house selects and handed to your callback.
items.docs: options lists the countries (leave countries out for all of them), the suggested countries that come first, the languages, each named in itself, and the currencies. Control it with region and onRegionChange, or let it keep the state with defaultRegion; either way the callback gets the full triple { country, language, currency } on every change and nothing navigates. The summary line says the choice in words, and the country names come from Intl.DisplayNames in the language of locale. Below md the group is one button, named by the summary, that opens a dialog with the same three fields. onRegionChange is a function, so use the footer from a Client Component or pass a Server Action. labels translates every visible word, the headings and the empty message of the country list included, navLabel names the footer navigation, and linkAs renders your router's Link.

items.name: locale-suggestion-bar
items.title: Locale suggestion bar
items.description: A polite bar that offers the local version of the site once, with Switch and Stay actions, and leaves remembering the answer to you.
items.docs: Decide when to show it, for instance when Accept-Language names a language you have a version in and the page is another, and store the answer yourself: the bar never redirects, never guesses from an IP address and removes itself on any choice, so render it only if you have not asked before. suggested carries the question and the words of the buttons in the suggested language (switchLabel, stayLabel and closeLabel are all required, so nothing on the bar is left in English by accident), and its code becomes the lang of the region, so every word on the bar is pronounced right. When the buttons do not fit side by side on a narrow screen, Stay drops under Switch instead of being cut off. Switch is a link to suggested.href, so linkAs can be your router's Link; onSwitch, onStay (which gets current) and onDismiss are where you store the choice. The bar slides in once, and instantly under reduced motion. The callbacks are functions, so use the bar from a Client Component or pass Server Actions.

items.name: smart-app-banner
items.title: Smart app banner
items.description: A smart banner for phones that points to your store app: icon, name, rating, one Get or Open button and a close, left to you.
items.docs: Give it the name, a pitch, the icon (or let it draw a monogram of the name), the rating with its count, and storeHref. When you know the app is installed, pass installed and openHref, a deep link such as atlas://home: the button then reads Open. onAction tells you which button was followed, and onDismiss is where you store the choice and keep the banner away for thirty days; the banner hides itself when it is closed. showOn is "phones" by default (below 640px), "tablets" (below 1024px) or "all", and position says which page edge it sits on, "top" or "bottom": it picks the border side and pads the banner for the notch or the home indicator when the page sets viewport-fit=cover, while you place the banner in your layout yourself. The rating is stars and words, "Rated 4.8 out of 5 from 12,400 reviews", with the numbers formatted for locale. This is for an app in a store; installing a web app is a different prompt. labels translates the fixed words.

items.name: navbar-two-row
items.title: Two-row navbar
items.description: A header in two rows: brand, search and account links on top, the categories underneath, scrolling sideways on a phone.
items.docs: Put the search field in search (a SearchTrigger, a form), the account, help and bag in utilities and the categories in categories; catalogue is the trailing link to everything. The header is sticky with a negative top, the height of the first row, so on scroll the first row slides away and only the categories stay: plain CSS, no scroll listener. While keyboard focus is inside the first row the whole bar unpins (CSS :has and :focus-visible), so a control you tab to is never out of sight above the window, and it pins again as soon as focus moves on. It counts on the first row's fixed height (56px on a phone, 48px more with the search row, 64px from md), so keep your mark within it, and it works when the header sits in the container that scrolls, the page or a layout of your own. Under md the search gets a row of its own and the categories are one scrolling line with fade edges and the current one brought into view. Mark the current page with currentHref, set sticky={false} to keep the bar in the flow, use linkAs for your router's Link and navLabel to name the categories landmark.

items.description: The top bar of a documentation site: brand, a row of section links, a search field and icon links, folding into a menu on a phone.

The sections are plain links, not an ARIA tablist, because each one goes to another page. onSearchOpen opens your own command palette from the field and from the shortcut (shortcutKey, Ctrl or Command and K), so use the header from a Client Component, next to the palette. links are icon links to the repository or the community: they open in a new tab and say so, and below md they fold into one menu. children is one compact control at the end of the first row, a theme toggle or a version select, and it stays on a phone. items.title: Docs page footer
items.description: The end of every docs page: an edit link, when it changed and who wrote it, a feedback slot, and previous and next cards that say where each goes.
items.docs: Pass editHref (where the page can be edited; it opens in a new tab and says so), updated ({ label, dateTime }: the label is the words, formatted on your side in the language and time zone of the page, and dateTime the same day for the time element), contributors ({ name, image }: up to four avatars with the total written beside them, and every name in a list only a screen reader gets), a feedback slot (keep its buttons in the page after a choice, as the demo does, so keyboard focus is not dropped), and previous and next ({ href, title }). items.name: page-header-split
items.title: Split page header
items.description: An inner-page opening in two columns: the title set very large on the left, the lede, up to four facts and one action on the right.

Below lg the columns stack with the title first. The facts follow the width of their column, not of the window: four share a row once their column is 448px wide, three once it is 384px, and until then they keep two to a row, so a value never wraps or runs into its neighbour. items.name: product-subnav
items.title: Product subnav
items.description: A product's local navigation: its name set large above the links, then a 56px sticky bar with the name, the links and one action once you scroll.
items.docs: Pass name, tagline, links ({ label, href }), an action, currentHref, mode, offset and linkAs. It renders two siblings, the intro and the bar, so put it directly in the element that holds the page: a sticky bar stays for as long as its parent is on screen. The intro is the name set large with the tagline (nameAs picks the element: p by default, h1 on the overview page). The bar is 56px from md up and sticks at offset pixels from the top, the height of your main navbar; once it has reached its place the name appears at its left, with the links in the middle and the action at the right. In pages mode (the default) the links go to the product's other pages and the current one carries aria-current="page". In anchors mode they are fragment links to sections of the page: the bar follows the scroll with aria-current="location", scrolls to a section with the navbar and the bar cleared (smoothly, or at once under reduced motion), and moves focus to its heading; give the sections a scroll-margin as tall as both for visitors who arrive with the hash in the address. On a phone the bar is two rows: the name above, and under it a row of links that scrolls sideways with fading edges and holds the action pinned at its right end, so the button stays level with the links before the name arrives and after. The links of pages mode are rendered on the server, so a Server Component can pass its router's Link as linkAs.

items.name: mobile-contact-bar
items.title: Mobile contact bar
items.description: A phone-only bar fixed to the bottom with Call, WhatsApp, Directions and Book as equal icon buttons, for local business sites.
items.docs: Pass two to four actions ({ kind, label, detail, href, external }): kind is call, whatsapp, directions, book or email and picks the icon, label is the short name, and detail is the number or the street written under it, so the action is clear to everyone and not only to people who read the icon (a number inside the label works too). Every action is a real link (tel:, a WhatsApp or maps address, your booking page), so it works without script. The bar is fixed to the bottom and hidden from md up; hideFrom takes another breakpoint, or never. It respects the safe-area inset, so add viewport-fit=cover to your viewport meta. While it shows it adds its own height to the bottom of the page (reserve={false} turns that off) and publishes the height as --contact-bar-height on the root, for a footer or a back-to-top button that must clear it. showAfter keeps it away until the visitor has scrolled that many pixels. It is out of the tab order and the accessibility tree while hidden, and under reduced motion it fades instead of sliding. Inside a preview frame or any pane that scrolls instead of the window, pass that element as scrollRoot (a ref).

items.description: A footer for regulated businesses: registration facts, the regulator statement, a risk notice and the legal links, set to be read.

items.name: footer-trust-marks
items.title: Trust marks footer
items.description: A footer with a row of quality marks and memberships drawn as quiet, named tiles, for businesses where credentials decide the sale.
items.docs: Pass the link columns and the marks ({ label, issuer, href, image, since }). A tile shows the issuer's artwork, greyed, when you pass image, and the issuer as a clean text mark when you do not; the issuer is the tile's accessible name, label sits under it, and since is written "Since 2014" (labels.since translates it). A mark with href links to its entry in the issuer's register and opens in a new tab. Every tile is one size, so mixed artwork lines up, and nothing animates. Artwork should be dark on a clear ground: the tile turns it grey, and light in the dark theme. From md up the tiles sit in a grid whose columns follow how many marks there are, so the last row is full: one row for four or five, three by two for six (one row of six from xl), two rows of four for seven or eight. On a phone the row scrolls sideways with fading edges, and when no mark is a link that row gets a focus stop of its own so the keyboard can scroll it; the grid, which does not scroll, never gets one. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

items.name: footer-split-panel
items.title: Split panel footer
items.description: A footer in two panels: an inverted card with the pitch and one action, and the link columns on the plain page beside it.
items.docs: Pass brand, statement, an action and social ({ label, href, icon }) for the card, the columns for the page beside it, and legal with legalLinks for the row beneath both. Inside the card the primary pair is turned round and the neutral tokens follow, so a plain Button or a focus ring is already the right way round, and a hairline sits just inside its edge. On a phone the card comes first and the columns follow two across. Profiles open in a new tab and say so; linkAs renders the internal links with your router's Link; labels translates the fixed words. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

items.name: family-sites-bar
items.title: Family sites bar
items.description: A slim strip above the header that lists the sibling sites of a group, with the current one marked and a link to the parent.
items.docs: Pass group ({ label, href }, written as it is read: "Part of Northwind"), the sites ({ label, href }), current (an href or a label) and an optional trailing link, usually to the group home. The strip is one navigation landmark named "Our sites"; the current site gets aria-current, weight, an underline and the words "Current site" for a screen reader. Sibling links open in the same tab, and every label stays on one line: from lg up a list that is wider than the room it has scrolls sideways with fading edges instead of wrapping, and the group keeps its whole name. Below lg the sites move into a button that opens a panel under the strip: a disclosure, closed by Escape, a click elsewhere, Tab leaving it or choosing a link, with the current site marked in plain words and the trailing link as its last row. linkAs renders the links with your router's Link; labels translates the fixed words. The server renders everything but the button's open state and the fade of the list.

items.name: navbar-floating
items.title: Floating navbar
items.description: A rounded bar that floats clear of the page edges, with a highlight that slides to the link you hover or the page you are on.
items.docs: Pass brand, flat items ({ label, href }), actions and currentHref. The pill is solid and bordered, centred with space on every side, and sticky by default so the page scrolls behind it; give it a negative bottom margin (className="-mb-[4.5rem]") when the hero should sit behind it. One highlight follows hover and focus along the links and settles on the current page when they leave; it is measured from the link boxes, so it fits any label, and under reduced motion it jumps instead of sliding. On a phone the pill shrinks to the brand and a menu button, and the links open as a panel under it: a disclosure closed by Escape, a click outside or choosing a link. linkAs renders the links with your router's Link, so a Server Component can use the bar.

items.name: navbar-fullscreen-menu
items.title: Fullscreen menu navbar
items.description: A bar with only the brand and a Menu button that opens a full-screen overlay of large numbered links and contact details.
items.docs: Pass brand, links ({ label, href, hint }), contact ({ address, email, phone, social }), currentHref and menuLabel. At rest the bar is only the brand and a Menu button, at every screen size. The button opens a full-screen overlay built on Dialog: focus moves in and stays there, Escape or the Close button leaves, and focus returns to the Menu button. The links are set in very large type under a two-digit index, the current one marked with aria-current and a dot, and while one is under the pointer or the keyboard the titles of the others soften to half strength (still 3:1 against the page); choosing a link closes the overlay. From sm up a hint sits at the right of its title in a column of its own, where it wraps (two lines at most) so that no row is taller than the others; below sm it sits under the title. The second column holds the address, the email and phone as links, and the profiles, which open in a new tab. The links arrive one after another with a short stagger, and simply appear under reduced motion. linkAs renders the links with your router's Link; labels translates the fixed words. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

items.name: navbar-side-rail
items.title: Side rail navbar
items.description: A navigation rail fixed to the left edge: the mark at the top, large vertical links, contact and profiles at the foot, and a top bar with a menu sheet on a phone.
items.docs: Wrap your page: <NavbarSideRail brand links footer currentHref>{page}</NavbarSideRail>. From lg up the rail is fixed to the left edge and the page sits beside it, padded by the rail width (width, default 16rem), which is also written on the root as --rail-width for your own full-bleed or fixed parts. links take label, href and an optional count; currentHref marks the current page with aria-current and a dot. footer takes email, social ({ label, href }) and a note, and sits at the foot of the rail and of the phone menu. Below lg the rail is a sticky top bar with the brand and a Menu button that opens a sheet with the same links. The rail is position: fixed, so the window must scroll (inside a frame, give the frame a transform). The page region is a main landmark: mainId names it for a skip link, contentAs="div" drops the landmark. linkAs renders the links with your router Link.

items.name: navbar-masthead
items.title: Masthead navbar
items.description: An editorial header in three tiers: a thin date and account line, the publication name set large in the middle, and the sections ruled below.
items.docs: Pass name (a string or your wordmark; nameHref makes it a link home), date (today's, from the server), locale and timeZone, sections ({ label, href }), actions (sign in and a subscribe button) and currentHref. The three tiers are siblings and the header is display: contents, so the top line and the sections are sticky for the whole page: put the header directly in the page's wrapper, not in a wrapper of its own. The name scrolls away behind the top line; there is no scroll handler. The date is written with Intl in the stated locale and time zone, so server and browser agree. Below md the sections scroll sideways with the current one brought into view and the date shortens. sticky={false} makes it an ordinary header. linkAs renders the section links with your router's Link.

items.name: section-dots-nav
items.title: Section dots nav
items.description: A slim rail of dots down the side of a long page, one per section, each a labelled link that marks where you are.
items.docs: Pass sections as { id, label } in page order: each becomes a dot linking to #id. The section in view is found with an IntersectionObserver and marked aria-current='location'; the last one takes over at the end of the page. A click scrolls smoothly (instantly under reduced motion) and moves focus to the section. offset is the height of a fixed header, side is 'left' or 'right', label names the navigation, and scrollContainer is a CSS selector for the element that scrolls when it is not the window. The rail is hidden below lg, where AnchorNav or a menu does the job. linkAs renders the dots with your router's Link.

items.name: footer-inverted-contact
items.title: Inverted contact footer
items.description: A dark footer led by one large email address, with the studio's details, profiles, sitemap and its local time beside them.
items.docs: Pass email (the large link; a long one breaks after the @), headline, address (lines), social, links (the sitemap) and legal. city with timeZone ('Europe/Amsterdam') adds the local-time line, and locale 'en-GB' writes it as 14:32. The clock renders after mount and is rewritten every minute; it is a time element with an accessible name, not a live region. A time zone the browser does not know shows the city without a clock, never a guessed time. The colours are primary and primary-foreground, so the footer is inverted in light and in dark. labels translate the fixed words. linkAs renders the sitemap links with your router's Link.

items.name: footer-curtain
items.title: Curtain footer
items.description: A footer that stays put while the page slides up over it, uncovering it like a curtain at the end of the scroll, in plain CSS.
items.docs: Wrap the page and give the footer: <FooterCurtain footer={<FooterSection … />}>{page}</FooterCurtain>. The page sits on an opaque raised layer and the footer is sticky to the bottom of the window beneath it. Keep the footer shorter than the window, or its top is cut off. minViewportHeight (default 640) is the window height below which the effect is off and the footer is an ordinary one; it is off in print too. Put it directly in the page's wrapper. Keyboard focus inside the footer lifts the curtain at once, so a focused link is never hidden under the page. It is pure CSS with no listener, so it works with native and with smooth scrolling.

items.name: print-letterhead
items.title: Print letterhead
items.description: The letterhead and running footer that appear only when a page is printed or saved as a PDF, with the site chrome taken off the paper.
items.docs: Render it once in your layout: <PrintLetterhead brand details url hideSelectors />. On screen it renders nothing. When printed it shows the letterhead (brand left, details right, a rule) and, in the bottom page margin of every page, a running footer: the address on the left and 'Printed <date> · Page 1 of 3' on the right. The footer is written into page margin boxes, outside the text area, so a list, a table or a paragraph can never print over it; Chromium prints margin boxes, and a browser without them prints no footer rather than one over the text. The stylesheet takes off navigation, the site header and footer (not those inside an article, main or section), dialogs, banners and anything marked data-print-hide, plus your hideSelectors; it removes backgrounds and shadows, prints the light palette in dark mode, writes the address after links inside the article (data-print-no-url opts out) and keeps headings and table rows whole. The date is written as printing starts, the only script. locale, timeZone and three labels translate the footer. Switch off the print dialog's own headers and footers to avoid doubles.

items.name: logo-strip
items.title: Logo strip
items.description: A single quiet row of customer marks with a short lead-in on the left, made to sit right under a hero without competing with it.
items.docs: Pass title, logos (the Logo type of LogoCloud: name, mark, href) and an optional more ({ label, href }) that sits under the lead-in. Marks are drawn at one height in the muted text colour; a linked mark comes to full strength on hover and has a focus ring, and a picture mark is greyed and dimmed. Every mark carries its name for screen readers. The strip answers to its own width, not the window: from 56rem, where six marks fit, the lead-in sits on the left and the marks spread across one row; narrower, the marks sit three to a row (two under 18rem), beside the lead-in down to 42rem and under it below that, so six make two even rows. Marks never shrink to an unreadable size. Put it directly under a hero.
