items.title: Testimonial list
items.description: Customer quotes set as editorial rows between hairlines: the words large on the left, the person and their result on the right.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional eyebrow, and testimonials ({ id, quote, name, role, company, avatar?, result? }). The list adds the quotation marks. A row is the quote on the left and the person on the right (portrait or initials, name, 'role, company'); result adds a chip that screen readers hear as 'Result: …', and labels.result translates that word. Hairlines divide the rows, on a phone each row is the quote and then the person, and nothing animates.

items.name: reviews-by-source
items.title: Reviews by source
items.description: Review cards with stars, title, date and reviewer, filtered by where they were written, with the average and count for each source.
items.docs: Pass reviews ({ id, source, rating, title, body, author, date }) and sources ({ name, average, count, href? }) in tab order. The summary under the tabs uses each source's own average and count, and for All the weighted average of them; it is a polite live region. A rating is read as 'Rated 4.5 out of 5' and drawn to the half star. href adds 'Read all on {source}'. value, defaultValue ('all' or a source's name) and onValueChange control the tab. locale and timeZone format numbers and dates; labels translate every fixed word (templates use {average}, {count}, {reviews}, {source}, {rating} and {max}). Source names are text, never logos.

items.title: Headline stat
items.description: One number set enormous with the sentence that explains it, backed by three smaller figures and an honest source line.

The figure is sized to its column from the length it will have, so '$128.4M' shrinks to fit. The final value is in the page from the first render, and under reduced motion nothing counts.

items.title: Press mentions list
items.description: In the news as a dated list: outlet, headline and date per row, every headline a link, with an optional limit and a show-all button.
items.docs: Pass items ({ outlet, headline, date, href, excerpt? }), title, locale and timeZone for the dates, and limit to show that many rows with a 'Show all coverage' button. The date and outlet sit in the left column and the headline is the link, though the whole row is the click target; a full http(s) address opens in a new tab with an arrow and 'opens in a new tab' for screen readers, a relative one stays in the tab. A date-only string is a calendar date and never shifts with the time zone. labels translate the three fixed texts.

items.name: quote-rail
items.title: Quote rail
items.description: Testimonial cards in one sideways rail that snaps card by card, with previous and next buttons, for more quotes than room, and nothing that moves by itself.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and items ({ id, quote, name, role, avatar?, rating? }); six to twelve read well. Cards share one readable width and one height, with the person pinned to the bottom. It is the browser's own scrolling with scroll snapping, so touch, trackpad and the arrow keys work with no script (the rail is a focusable list named by the heading) and nothing ever autoplays. Two round buttons step one card back or on and rest at the ends (aria-disabled, still in the tab order); they sit at the end of the heading row from 640px and under the heading on a phone, so the title keeps the full width; after a press a polite live region says 'Quote 3 of 9' or 'Quotes 3 to 5 of 9', and a thin line with a count under the rail shows the position. On a phone the rail runs to the screen edge so the next card peeks in: set --rail-gutter on the section to your page's side padding (default 1.5rem). labels carries the fixed words, locale the numbers.

items.name: logo-groups
items.title: Logo groups
items.description: Customers grouped by industry or segment under small headings, so an enterprise buyer finds the sector that matters in one glance.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and groups ({ title, count, logos, href? }). Logos use the Logo type of LogoCloud (name, mark, href); every mark is drawn at one height in the muted text colour and comes to full strength on hover and focus, and each keeps its company name for screen readers. count is written as you want it ('38 customers'); give a group href and the count becomes a link to that sector's customer list, named 'in {sector}' for screen readers (labels.inGroup translates it). Groups sit in two columns from 640px and one on a phone, cut apart by hairlines; an odd last group spans both columns. From 1024px the marks of each group sit on a two-column grid (four in a row for a group that spans), so four marks make a tidy two by two and the groups line up with each other; below that they wrap. A mark with no image or SVG is set as text in a muted tone that still meets AA contrast. Renders on the server.

items.name: video-testimonials
items.title: Video testimonials
items.description: Customer video cards with a poster, a visible play button and the length; a press opens the video in an accessible dialog and stops it on close.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and videos ({ id, name, role, poster, src?, duration, captions? }); three is the layout it is made for. A card is one real button named like "Play Maria's story, 2 minutes 14 seconds" (spoken with Intl; labels.play translates it), with the poster always visible, a play disc, and the name, role and length as text. Nothing about the video is fetched before the press. A press opens a Dialog with a native video (controls, preload none, a captions track from captions: { src, lang, label? } switched on) and starts it; closing pauses it, Escape closes, and focus returns to the card. A video that fails shows a message. A card whose poster is missing or fails to load shows the initials in a small tile in the corner, and keeps the middle for the play button; give posters open ground in the middle (the speaker off to one side). To host the video elsewhere pass renderPlayer(video) returning your embed (className="absolute inset-0 size-full"): it only mounts when its card is pressed. Only the card is a client component.

items.name: customer-results-table
items.title: Customer results table
items.description: Results per customer in a real table: who, their industry, the metric before and after, and how long it took.
items.docs: Pass title, rows ({ customer, mark?, industry, metric, before, after, change, period, href? }) and caption, which is required: say where the numbers come from and how they were measured. Figures are strings written as you want them. After is set heavier with the signed change beside it as a chip (a leading minus or plus adds a trend arrow, and screen readers hear 'change -41%'); the chip has a column of its own, so a long change such as '+12.5 percentage points' widens that column and never overprints its neighbour; every figure uses tabular digits. A row with href makes the customer name a link. From 768px it is a real table named by the heading, with header cells and a row header per customer and the caption under it; below that each row is a card that leads with the outcome (the metric under the name, then before and after on one line with the change beside it, then the industry and the time in a quiet line) and gives every value its label to screen readers, so a phone never scrolls sideways. mark is a small mark drawn at about 16px in a tile; without it the tile holds the first letter. labels carries the column names. Renders on the server.

items.title: Claim quotes
items.description: Each claim you make (fast setup, honest pricing, real support) backed by a customer quote and, where you have one, a number.

Each claim is an article with a heading, a description-list figure and a blockquote, so a screen reader hears the claim, the number, then the evidence. From 768px the articles share rows through a subgrid, so headings, figures, quotes and attributions line up across the row however long any quote is, and every number sits at the top of its row however many lines its label takes; a claim without a figure leaves its row empty rather than shifting the rest. On a phone every claim is a full-width block under its own rule. The block adds the quotation marks. Renders on the server.

items.title: Testimonials by role
items.description: Let visitors hear from people like them: role or industry chips narrow a grid of quotes, and the count is announced.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description, testimonials ({ id, quote, name, role, group, avatar? }) and groups (the chip labels after All; each quote's group must equal one of them). The chips are one toggle group with exactly one pressed, so the arrow keys move between them and pressing the pressed chip keeps it; the count under them ('4 of 12 quotes', labels.count) is a polite live region. Quotes sit in balanced columns at their natural height, with as many columns as the filter leaves quotes for (one quote is centred at a readable width, two or four fill two columns, three or more fill three from 1024px), so a short result never hugs one side; they swap with a crossfade while the section glides to its new height, so nothing jumps; reduced motion swaps at once. items.title: Logo results grid
items.description: A customer wall where every logo carries one line of outcome and a link to the story, so each name earns its place.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and items ({ name, mark?, result, metric?, href? }); six to nine read best, and a count that does not tile still ends on a full row. Each hairline cell shows the mark (an SVG or image drawn about 28px tall in the text colour; the name is set as text without one), the result in plain words and, with an href, a quiet 'Read the story' arrow. The figure inside the result is medium weight in tabular digits: give metric exactly as it appears in result ('41 percent'), or leave it out and the first number with its unit is used. A cell with an href is one link as a whole (focus ring inside, the arrow moves on hover); a cell without one is not a link and has no arrow. Three columns from 1024px, two from 640px, one on a phone; when the last row is short, its last cell stretches across the free columns (all three for a seventh, two for an eighth, both on two columns for an odd one), so no blank cell is left behind. labels.readStory translates the arrow line. items.name: satisfaction-scores
items.title: Satisfaction scores
items.description: An overall score and category scores as labelled bars, the way buyers compare tools, with the source and a method link built in.
items.docs: Pass overall ({ score, max, responses, period }), categories ({ label, score }; five or six), source (required) and methodHref, plus an optional title and description. The overall number is plain, large text in tabular digits. Every category is a role="meter" with label, range and value, so assistive technology reads 'Ease of use, 9.4 out of 10' once and the drawing is left out of the reading. The server renders the bars full, and a list on screen when the page opens stays full; once the reader scrolls, a list still below the window fills its bars once, a little after one another, as it comes into view. Reduced motion and print show everything at rest. The source and the method link are part of the API on purpose: a score without them undermines itself. decimals sets the digits, locale the numbers, labels the fixed words.

items.name: benchmark-bars
items.title: Benchmark bars
items.description: Prove a claim against the field: your customers' result beside the industry median for each metric, as paired bars with the multiple in words.
items.docs: Pass title, metrics ({ id, label, ours: { value, label? }, benchmark: { value, label? }, unit?, better, comparative? }), source (required) and methodHref. Each metric has its own scale: two bars (your customers in the foreground tone, the benchmark muted), both values written at the bar ends in tabular digits (keep them short: past 14 characters a value may wrap beside its bar, and the values never take more than 45% of a row, so a bar never collapses), and the multiple in words worked out from the same numbers ('7.4 times faster'; comparative picks the word when you win, otherwise 'higher' or 'lower'). With better: "lower" the shorter bar wins and a note says so; within 5 percent it reads 'in line with the median'; a result that trails is described as it is. Each metric is a figure whose caption reads the whole comparison to a screen reader. The bars are full on the server and on screen at load; a row still below the window grows once as it comes into view. Reduced motion and print show them at rest. labels sets the words.

items.name: review-topics
items.title: Review topics
items.description: What reviewers mention most: topics with how often and how positively, each opening to a real snippet rather than an invented summary.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description and topics ({ id, label, mentions, positive, snippet: { quote, author } }); five to eight read well, most mentioned first. A row shows the topic, 'mentioned in 842 reviews' and a bar for the share of positive mentions (0 to 1) with the percentage written beside it followed by the word 'positive' (small and muted, labels.positive), so '94%' always says what it is the share of, for everyone. Each row is a disclosure on the Accordion primitive: it opens to one verbatim snippet and its author, and only one row stays open at a time; the content glides open and shut unless reduced motion is on. A row tints quietly on hover, and the bars are decoration in the foreground tone, so the list reads in monochrome and in dark mode. Uncontrolled with defaultValue (a topic id), or controlled with value and onValueChange. locale formats the numbers, labels the fixed words.

items.name: expert-endorsements
items.title: Expert endorsements
items.description: Quotes from doctors, chefs and coaches with their qualification as real text, a required disclosure and a Sponsored badge for paid voices.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description, experts ({ id, name, credential, quote, affiliation?, photo?, href?, sponsored? }) and disclosure. The disclosure is required and printed under the grid, because endorsements are regulated in many markets: say whether the experts were paid, or which of them were; pass null only when you have checked that nothing needs saying. An expert with sponsored: true carries a solid Sponsored badge on the top edge of the card and a rel="sponsored" link. The credential is a chip of real text that a screen reader hears as 'Credential: Dermatologist, MD', never part of the picture, and the portrait shows at once (initials, without a title such as Dr., stand in until it loads). Two to six experts; three sit in a row on a desktop, four sit two by two, and an odd last card spans the width on a tablet. labels carries the fixed words.

items.name: customer-photo-grid
items.title: Customer photo grid
items.description: A tight grid of customer photos, each linking to the original post, with the handle and caption on the tile and a call to share yours.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description, photos ({ id, photo, alt, handle, caption?, href }), an optional cta ({ label, href }) and an optional permission line ('Shared with permission'). Three across on a desktop and two on a phone. The strip under every photo is the link to the original post: it is named by the handle and the caption, exactly what is written on it, and it stretches over the whole tile so the photo is part of the target. The handle and caption are always visible, never on hover only, and the handle wraps on a narrow tile instead of being cut short; the alt text, which is required, describes the picture. Photos are cropped to a square through AspectRatio, so nothing shifts as they load, and they load lazily. The call to action is a Button link; permission is plain text next to it.

The two images share one aspect ratio (4:3, or set ratio to 3/4 for portrait work) so the pair lines up, each carries a Before or After label in its corner as text on a solid chip, never colour alone, and on a phone the pair stacks with the labels intact. There is no slider and no animation, so the comparison is immediate; the chips keep their fill when printed without background graphics. details is the list of what was done; timeframe is read as 'Time it took: 6 weeks'. labels carries the fixed words.

A lg tier shows large tiles with the mark, the name and a line; md a compact hairline grid of marks whose short last row grows to fill the width; sm supporters as avatars with names in columns (avatar is an image URL, initials stand in without one; the avatar is only decoration, so a link is read as the name alone). Tier names are h3 headings, a tier without sponsors is left out, each sponsor with an href is one link named by its text, and sponsoredLinks adds rel="sponsored" to every link when the sponsorship is paid. items.name: review-form
items.title: Review form
items.description: Collect a review or testimonial: stars, headline, story, name and an unticked permission to publish, with busy, sent and error states announced.
items.docs: Pass onSubmit(review) (it may return a promise), title and an optional description. The review is { rating, headline, story, name, role, email, photo, consent }; rating, story, first name and consent are required, the rest optional, and fields switches the role field (on by default) and the photo field (off; it is a Choose a photo button with a small preview, the file name and a button to take the picture away again). Consent starts unchecked and says exactly what may be published; privacy replaces the line under it (a sensible default is built in; pass links to your privacy page). Problems appear under the field, the field is marked invalid and described by its message (the stars, the story and the consent box as well as the text fields), and focus goes to the first one. While the promise is pending the fields lock and the button shows a spinner; when it resolves the confirmation replaces the form in place, takes focus and shows what was sent, with after for the next step; when it rejects an alert appears above the button and takes focus, one Tab from trying again, and every value is kept for another try. A polite live region announces sending, sent and the problems found. To drive the state yourself (a server action, a mutation) pass status ('idle' | 'busy' | 'done' | 'error') and error; defaultValues pre-fills the fields and restores a form after a failed server action. labels carries every fixed word, so the form can speak any language.

items.title: Logo quote popovers
items.description: A logo wall where each customer opens a small panel with their quote, name and result, on click or tap and not on hover alone.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional description ('Select a logo to read what they said.') and customers ({ id, name, mark?, quote, person, role?, result?, href? }). Every mark is a button that opens a Popover anchored to it; the marks sit in the muted text colour with a small plus that turns into a cross, and the open one is full strength with aria-expanded. Only one panel is open at a time, Escape or the close button closes it and focus returns to the mark; when a panel opens, focus moves to the panel, which is named for the customer. Because it opens on press it works on touch and with a keyboard, which a hover card does not. The panel holds the quote, the person, their role and an optional result line that links to the story when href is set. Which panel is open is state you can own: pass openId (a customer id, or null) with onOpenChange(id | null) to control it, or defaultOpenId to start with one open, which is how a preview shows a quote; a panel that starts open, or that the page opens, does not take focus. labels carries the fixed words, with {name} filled in.

items.title: Quote stack
items.description: Short lines of praise set as large type and stacked down the page with small attributions; the line you point at stays at full strength.
items.docs: Pass title and quotes ({ id, quote, name, role }); four to six one-sentence quotes under fifteen words each read best. On a wide screen the quotes alternate between the left and the right two thirds of the width; on a phone they sit in one left-aligned column. While the pointer is over one quote, or keyboard focus is on it, the others dim to 40 percent with a CSS selector on the list: no script, no motion, and on a touch screen everything stays at full strength. A quote and the air around it are one hover target, so the pointer hands over from one quote to the next and the stack never flashes back to full strength in between. Each quote is in the tab order unless focusable is false. It is a real list of figures that reads in any order.

items.name: proof-bento
items.title: Proof bento
items.description: One grid for all your proof: a large quote, a stat that counts up, a rating, a row of customer logos and a photo, in tiles of mixed size.
items.docs: Pass title, an optional eyebrow and description, and tiles: objects told apart by kind. quote { quote, name, role?, avatar? } sets the words large with the person under them (the tile adds the quotation marks). stat { value, label, detail?, prefix?, suffix?, decimals? } shows one figure; a number counts up once as it scrolls into view, text such as '24/7' is set as written. rating { score, count, source, max?, href? } draws stars to the fraction and is read as one sentence ('Rated 4.8 out of 5 on G2, 2,140 reviews'); with an href the whole tile is one link. logos { title?, logos } takes the same { name, mark?, href? } as LogoCloud; every mark keeps its own width, so a narrow tile wraps them in a row and a wide one sets them in columns, and a wordmark is never squeezed into a cell. image { src, alt, caption, credit?, focalPoint? } fills the tile with a photo and puts the caption on a solid chip, so it reads on any picture; alt is required. Every tile has an id and takes span (1 or 2 of the four columns) and rowSpan (1 or 2 rows, from a desktop up). Tiles are placed in the order you give and never reordered, so the DOM order is the reading order: pair the spans until each row of four is full. Below a desktop (1024px) there are two columns and row spans are ignored, and a single tile that would be left alone in its row takes the whole row, so there is never a hole (a one-column quote that gets a row to itself is set at the wider size there). A quote is set largest on two columns and two rows, smaller on two columns and smallest on one, so give a one-column quote one short sentence. Figures are sized to their tile from the longest figure of that width, so '99.98%' fits and a row of stats stays level; counting is skipped under reduced motion and the final value is in the page from the first render. locale sets digits and separators (a tag the browser cannot read, such as 'en_US', falls back to en-US); labels carries the fixed words.
